I think what they mean is that a small amount of inflation is already baked into the system. For example, part of the reason a bank will charge a 3% interest rate on a mortgage is because they expect inflation. With 2% inflation then your 3% interest rate is really more like the interest is covering the loss of the purchasing power on the money you borrowed, plus another 1% to serve as the rental payment for borrowing money.

If there is 1% deflation then it's like you're paying a whole 4% rent on the money you borrowed, and you'll be stuck doing that until interest rates fall enough to allow you to refinance. If you want an example of this look at historical inflation rates and interest rates. The expected inflation rate was much higher in the 60's and 70's but then in 1981 Paul Volker (who was Reagan's federal reserve chairman) and Reagan reset things and stopped printing so much money every year. It triggered a short recession but the economy was healthier afterward because of it.
